title: Haemoglobin mass: how much, for whom, and does it help?
goal: Estimate the Hb mass gain from a camp, judge what shapes the response, and weigh the placebo-controlled evidence on sea-level performance.

steps.title: About 1% per 100 hours
steps.text:
The best single number comes from a [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 17 studies that measured [haemoglobin mass](g:haemoglobin-mass) by [CO rebreathing](g:co-rebreathing) before, during and after altitude: about **+1.1% per 100 h** of exposure, for both classic altitude and LHTL [[c:hb-rate-claim]]. After the camp, Hb mass stayed about 3.3% above baseline for up to 20 days. The authors judged that camps as short as 2 weeks quite likely raise Hb mass and most athletes can expect benefit [[c:hb-camp]].

The unit is hours, not days: dose counts. The straight-line rule describes the camps that were studied; it is not a promise for any single athlete (see the card on noise).

claims.text: During altitude exposure, haemoglobin mass rises about 1.1% per 100 h (LHTL and classic altitude), and was 3.3% above baseline for up to 20 days afterwards.

evidence.quote: During-altitude Hbmass was estimated to increase by ∼1.1%/100 h for LHTL and classic altitude. Postaltitude Hbmass was estimated to be 3.3% higher than prealtitude values for up to 20 days.

claims.text: Camps as short as 2 weeks of classic altitude or LHTL will quite likely raise Hb mass.

evidence.quote: Camps as short as 2 weeks of classic and LHTL altitude will quite likely increase Hbmass and most athletes can expect benefit.

steps.title: Hb mass after a camp
steps.problem: An athlete has 800 g of Hb mass. He spends 12 h·day⁻¹ in a tent for 28 days. How much Hb mass do you expect at the end?
steps: 800 × 1.037 = 829.6 g, about 830 g (a gain of about 30 g).

steps.title: From grams to VO₂max
steps.text:
What does a gain in Hb mass buy? Changing Hb mass by 1 g changes VO₂max by about 4 mL·min⁻¹ [[c:hb-slope]] (estimates run from 3 to 4). Divide by body mass to get the number athletes quote.

For 30 g in a 70 kg athlete: 30 × 4 = 120 mL·min⁻¹; 120 ÷ 70 = 1.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. That is about 2–3% of a VO₂max of 65, the same order as the 2.2 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ average LHTL gain in athletes in the paper of 21 October 2026. Real results vary because VO₂max also depends on the heart, muscle and, at altitude, on what you lose from the thin air.

claims.text: Changing Hb mass by 1 g alters VO₂max by about 4 mL·min⁻¹.

evidence.quote: Changes in hemoglobin mass by 1g alter V˙O2max by ∼4mL·mn-1 due to changes in blood volume or hemoglobin concentration.

steps.title: Grams to mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹
steps.problem: An athlete of 70 kg gains 30 g of Hb mass. Using 4 mL·min⁻¹ per g, what is the VO₂max gain?

steps.title: Dose and iron decide the response
steps.text:
More altitude is not always better. In 48 runners living at 1,780 to 2,800 m, [red-cell volume](g:red-cell-volume) rose in all four groups and did not differ between groups, yet 3,000-m time improved only at the two middle altitudes [[c:hb-chapman]].

Iron is the other limit: red cells need it. A review reports a study in which pre-altitude iron deficiency ([ferritin](g:ferritin) below 30 ng·mL⁻¹ in men, 20 in women) led to no gain in red cell volume [[c:hb-iron]], and says ferritin should be checked before and during the camp. Take iron only on the advice of a doctor, guided by blood tests.

claims.text: In 48 runners at four living altitudes, red-cell volume rose in every group, equally, but time-trial gains appeared only at 2,085 and 2,454 m.

evidence.quote: Erythrocyte volume was significantly higher within all groups after return from altitude and was not different between groups.

claims.text: Pre-altitude iron deficiency (ferritin below 30 ng·mL⁻¹ in men, 20 in women) was followed by no gain in red cell volume at altitude.

evidence.quote: pre-altitude iron deficiency (serum ferritin <30 ng/ml in men and <20 ng/ml in women) led to no improvements in RCV in responses to altitude exposure.
Therefore, ferritin levels must be monitored on a regular basis before and during the hypoxic exposure if the aim of altitude training is to improve blood oxygen-carrying capacity.

steps.title: Responders, noise and the fade
steps.text:
Averages hide people. For an athlete exposed to 300 h, the meta-analysis gave a 95% [prediction interval](g:prediction-interval) of 1.1–6% for the true Hb mass response [[c:hb-pi]]. The test itself is noisy: the within-person SD was about 2% over a week, which the authors call analytical error. So a measured +2% in one athlete is within the noise [[c:hb-noise-claim]].

The EPO response differs too: a review reports a study in which runners who did not improve their 5,000 m time had smaller EPO rises after 30 h of hypoxia than those who did [[c:hb-epo-resp]]. And gains fade: after coming down, the youngest red cells may be broken down quickly ([neocytolysis](g:neocytolysis)) [[c:hb-neo]].

claims.text: For 300 h of altitude, the 95% prediction interval for an athlete's true Hb mass response was 1.1–6%.

evidence.quote: A 95% prediction interval for the 'true' response of an athlete exposed to 300 h of altitude was estimated to be 1.1-6%.

claims.text: The within-subject SD of Hb mass measurements was about 2% for up to 7 days, indicating analytical error.

evidence.quote: The within-subject SD was constant at ∼2% for up to 7 days between observations, indicative of analytical error.

claims.text: In a study reported in a review, runners who improved their 5,000 m time had larger EPO rises after 30 h of hypoxia than those who did not.

evidence.quote: It was found that the responders had significantly larger increases in mean EPO concentration after 30 h of hypoxia compared to the non-responders.

claims.text: Some athletes showed signs of rapid red blood cell destruction after LHTL.

evidence.quote: concluded that there was evidence of rapid red blood cell destruction, at least in some athletes.

steps.title: Does it work at sea level? The placebo problem
steps.text:
Hb mass rises, but does race performance? Most studies could not blind athletes to altitude, and a meta-analysis found that effects were mediated at least partly by [placebo](g:placebo), nocebo and training-camp effects [[c:hb-bonetti]].

One team ran a [double-blind](g:blinding) test: 16 cyclists slept 16 h·day⁻¹ for 4 weeks in rooms with either normal air (placebo, n = 6) or normobaric hypoxia simulating 3,000 m (n = 10). They did not know their group; Hb mass, VO₂max and time-trial power stayed unchanged in both groups [[c:hb-sieb]]. A review notes the gold-standard design has never been done as a [crossover](g:crossover-study) [[c:hb-lundby]].

claims.text: Meta-analysed effects of altitude protocols were mediated partly by placebo, nocebo and training-camp effects, with natural LHTL the best protocol.

evidence.quote: There was evidence that these effects were mediated at least partly by substantial placebo, nocebo and training-camp effects with some protocols.
In summary, natural LHTL currently provides the best protocol for enhancing endurance performance in elite and subelite athletes, while some artificial protocols are effective in subelite athletes.

claims.text: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study (16 cyclists, 4 weeks, 16 h·day⁻¹ at a simulated 3,000 m), LHTL changed neither Hb mass nor time-trial power.

evidence.quote: Hb mass, maximal oxygen uptake (VO(2)) in normoxia, and at a simulated altitude of 2,500 m and mean power output in a simulated, 26.15-km time trial remained unchanged in both groups throughout the study.
Questionnaires revealed that subjects were unaware of group classification.

claims.text: A double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover trial of altitude training has never been conducted.

evidence.quote: For example, the scientific gold-standard design of a double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over trial has never been conducted on altitude training.

debate.question: Does LHTL improve sea-level performance beyond placebo and training-camp effects?

sides.position: Yes: natural LHTL gave the best gains in a 51-study meta-analysis, and Hb mass rises about 1.1% per 100 h; the open trials still leave placebo effects unmeasured.

Not shown: the one double-blind placebo-controlled study found no change in Hb mass or performance, and a review urges more scepticism. Its small groups and 16 h·day⁻¹ dose limit what it can rule out.

points: Hb mass rises about 1.1% per 100 h of altitude (LHTL or classic), about 3.3% above baseline for up to 20 days after; 1 g of Hb mass is worth about 4 mL·min⁻¹ of VO₂max.
The response depends on dose and on iron status: low ferritin before the camp means little or no red-cell gain.
Individual true responses vary (1.1–6% for 300 h) and the test's noise is about 2%, so one athlete's small change is not proof.
Whether LHTL beats placebo at sea level is disputed: open trials and a meta-analysis say yes; the one double-blind study found nothing, with small groups and a lower dose.

variants.stem: An athlete has 900 g of Hb mass and spends 14 h·day⁻¹ in a tent for 21 days. Using 1.1% per 100 h, what Hb mass do you expect at the end?

options.why: Applied 1.1% once, ignoring the hours of exposure.
Read 1.1% as per day (21 days): 900 × 1.231.
Gave the gain, not the final Hb mass.

options.why: Applied 1.1% once, ignoring the hours of exposure.
Read 1.1% as per day (28 days).
Gave the gain, not the final Hb mass.

variants.stem: A 70 kg athlete gains 29 g of Hb mass. Using 4 mL·min⁻¹ per g, what is the VO₂max gain?

options.why: Forgot to divide by body mass.
Correct: 29 × 4 ÷ 70.
Forgot the 4 mL·min⁻¹ per g: 29 ÷ 70.

options.why: Forgot to divide by body mass.
Forgot the 4 mL·min⁻¹ per g: 41 ÷ 75.
Correct: 41 × 4 ÷ 75.

variants.stem: In 48 runners, red cell volume rose equally at living altitudes of 1,780, 2,085, 2,454 and 2,800 m, but 3,000-m time improved only at 2,085 and 2,454 m. What does this show?

options.text: Red cell volume alone does not explain who got faster
options.why: Correct: the red cell gain was the same in all groups, so something else differed.

options.text: Altitudes above 2,500 m stop red cells forming
options.why: Red cell volume rose in the 2,800 m group as much as in the others.

options.text: The 1,780 m group did not acclimatise at all
options.why: Its red cell volume rose, though its EPO was back to baseline after 72 h.

variants.stem: A female runner's ferritin is 15 ng·mL⁻¹ six weeks before an altitude camp. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Tell her doctor and treat the low iron stores before the camp
options.why: Correct: low stores before altitude were linked to no red-cell gain; treatment goes through a doctor.

options.text: Go as planned: altitude itself will fix the iron
options.why: Altitude raises demand for iron; it does not fill the stores.

options.text: Take a large iron dose without a test, to be safe
options.why: Iron without testing or advice can harm; check and follow a doctor.

variants.stem: After a 300 h camp an athlete's Hb mass is measured 2.0% higher than before. The test's within-person SD is about 2%. What do you conclude?

options.text: She responded: any rise proves it
options.why: A 2% change equals the test's own noise.

options.text: The change is within test noise: it neither proves nor rules out a response
options.why: Correct: with 2% noise, one small change cannot be read as real.

options.text: She is a non-responder because the rise is under 3.3%
options.why: 3.3% is an average; the true individual range is 1.1–6%, and 2% sits inside it.

variants.stem: Per the meta-analysis, about how far above baseline was Hb mass after descent, and for how long?

options.text: About 3.3% above, for up to 20 days
options.why: Correct: the post-altitude estimate.

options.text: About 10% above, for up to 3 months
options.why: Far above the estimate: the gain fades within weeks.

options.text: About 1.1% above, for up to a year
options.why: Mixes the per-100 h rate with the post-camp level and duration.

options.text: Back to baseline on the day of descent
options.why: Hb mass stays raised for some weeks, though it may fade quickly in some athletes.

variants.stem: Why does a double-blind, placebo-controlled LHTL study matter?

options.text: A blinded placebo group separates belief from physiology
options.why: Correct: a group in the same rooms with normal air removes expectation and camp effects.

options.text: It makes the two groups the same size and load
options.why: Blinding does not set group size (here 10 against 6).

options.text: It measures Hb mass with less test error
options.why: Blinding affects bias, not measurement error.

variants.stem: The double-blind LHTL study found no change in Hb mass or performance. What limits how far it settles the question?

options.text: Athletes knew which group they were in, so results are biased
options.why: Questionnaires showed they were unaware of their group.

options.text: Small groups (10 and 6) and 16 h·day⁻¹, below the 22 h·day⁻¹ one group recommends
options.why: Correct: small numbers and a lower dose mean it cannot rule out a benefit at other doses.

options.text: Placebo-controlled studies are never valid for altitude
options.why: They are the gold-standard way to separate belief from physiology.
